title: Code erodes as agents build on their own work
summary: Each agent change on top of earlier agent changes adds a little duplication and complexity. Better prompts set a better starting point but don't stop the slide; only refactoring and review do. Whether newer models maintain code better is disputed: one measure shows fast gains, another the same decay across model tiers. In a controlled hand-off, code written with AI assistants was no harder for the next developer to change, so the slide may come from volume and repeated agent edits rather than any single change. Features keep landing at a steady pace, but breakage of earlier work does not fall, and early breakage compounds.

title: You can't tell from a task how well the agent will do
summary: Agents fail on tasks unlike what they were trained on, not on tasks that look hard. A task that seems easy can fail and a hard one succeed, so judge from real results on your work. Even small, irrelevant changes to a task's wording or numbers can flip the result.

title: Every line in the context file costs money
summary: Agents do follow context-file instructions, which means each mention of a tool or step gets acted on, every task. Extra instructions raise spend even when they don't help, and whether context files help at all is disputed: one source finds time saved, another no gain in success.

title: Agents act on outdated facts
summary: When a fact changes, agents often keep using the old version from memory or context files. Updated decisions need to replace, not sit beside, the old ones. Building the update into every task may keep notes current, but even its advocates still trim them by hand. A second pass that checks notes against session logs fixed a wrong note in one vendor test, but nobody has compared it with writing notes as you go.

title: Agreeable answers mislead without being wrong
summary: Assistants tend to agree with the person asking and pick facts that support them. Each statement can be true while the overall picture is skewed, and people rate these answers as more objective.

title: Review load lands on senior engineers
summary: PR volume has grown several times over while reviewer numbers haven't, so the extra review falls on the few people trusted to approve. Some teams move trust into tests and production checks and auto-merge part of their changes instead (one open-source maintainer says tests and scanners sort the pull requests); whether that holds up isn't known yet.

title: People follow AI advice they know is wrong
summary: Even reviewers who spot a flaw in an AI recommendation often go along with it. Spotting a problem isn't enough; reviewers need the time and the authority to reject. At the repository level the picture is less clear: review got faster and approved more often after agents arrived, but just as much in repositories without agents, so the agent may not be the cause. In a controlled review, labelling a suggested change as AI-written made no difference to how often a wrong one was accepted; harder code did.

title: Nobody knows how often agents leak secrets
summary: Leak rates are measured under planted attacks, and by one scan of public repos where an agent's saved approval rules held secrets; private repos and other agents are unmeasured. Plan for it as a likely risk; keep secrets out of reach. (OWASP LLM02, LLM07, 2025)

title: Prompt injection has no proven fix
summary: The one architecture shown to block most injection attacks has only been tested by its own authors, who say the problem isn't solved, and a guardrail that stops most attacks still fails by security standards. Limit what an agent can do rather than hoping it can't be tricked; whether an agent should ever approve its own change is still open. (OWASP LLM01, 2025) In tests on coding agents with no approval step, injected instructions were acted on in a large share of runs, and agents rarely said they had noticed one.

title: Test loops fix the code, not a misread requirement
summary: Letting an agent iterate against tests repairs edge cases and type errors, but if it misunderstood what was asked, it stays misunderstood. Only a person checking intent catches that.

title: Supervising agents needs the skills agents erode
summary: Checking agent code well takes hands-on coding skill, and relying on agents can wear that skill down. Without deliberate practice, a team loses the ability to review what it ships. Nobody knows yet whether the loss reverses or how to measure it; one theoretical model suggests that past a point, easing off isn't enough to recover, so protect unaided practice early.

title: Juniors ask the model instead of colleagues
summary: Most of a junior engineer's questions now go to an assistant rather than a teammate, and entry-level hiring is shrinking. The quick answer replaces the conversation where they would have learned how the team works, and nobody yet knows how juniors will grow into seniors. Students in team projects, though, used AI for their own preparation and kept it out of feedback, conflict and accountability.

title: Shared agent memory behaves like a shared database
summary: Team context files, skills and memory stores can leak data, go stale, hide contradictions and lose track of who wrote what. Nobody has settled how conflicting writes should be handled.

title: Pairing with AI isn't the same as pairing with a person
summary: Results on pairing with an assistant disagree, and some show lower quality than a human pair. It also skips the knowledge sharing that pairing exists for. With a human partner, more knowledge changes hands and more of it is questioned; alone with an assistant, more is accepted on trust. For novices, results can point the other way: they scored higher with an assistant than with a human partner and kept as much a week later, though they enjoyed it less.

title: Test-first results may not hold on current models
summary: The evidence that writing tests first helps agents comes from one language and from models that predate current ones, and only a lab re-check on small exercises has been done since. Vague requirements, where test-first is said to help most as a way of thinking, haven't been tried with agents. On newer models, an agent that writes tests first and revises both tests and code beat a plain loop, but the gain came from the revision loop, not the ordering, and most of its failures passed its own tests.

title: Nobody agrees what the human bottleneck is now
summary: With agents writing the code, practitioners disagree on whether verification, judgement, understanding or shared agreement on why a change exists becomes the constraint. Each position rests on one person's experience or opinion. One AI review vendor lets trusted engineers skip review and puts them back under review after outages they cause. One large vendor reads it differently: coding got faster, but choosing what to change, review and production operations did not, so the whole lifecycle gains little.

title: Strong engineering foundations may not protect you
summary: One industry survey says good practices partly shield teams from AI's downsides; telemetry across many companies finds no outcome protected. Don't assume a mature process makes agent adoption safe; watch your own delivery numbers.

title: Nobody knows how much to specify up front
summary: Giving agents more tests up front helped only to a point, and agents that designed before coding did better, so heavy spec-first work risks repeating waterfall. Another objection: a spec written whole before building assumes the system is finished once it does what the spec says, and software that keeps changing is not. Others argue the spec is the lasting artifact and should be executable; the evidence doesn't settle it.

title: Planning and execution prompts may need different detail
summary: One practitioner argues for goals-only planning prompts and fully detailed execution prompts. It is an opinion nobody has tested.

title: Fresh or continued context in agent loops is unsettled
summary: Some loops reset the agent's context every iteration; one comparison on a single task found continuing did better for the cost. Nobody has compared them on real work.

title: Nobody knows if multi-agent orchestration scales
summary: Adding agents may run into the same coordination cost as adding people to a late project (Brooks's Law), and more agents on unclear requirements may only give the wrong answer faster. One team saw agents coordinate through shared plans, at the cost of CI load. In controlled runs, messaging between agents levelled off as teams grew, naming one agent coordinator in the prompt changed nothing, and agents that saw each other's commits did better; none of it has been tested on real team projects.

title: It's unclear how much of a system a team must understand
summary: One view holds that a team's understanding of its system can't be rebuilt from documents once lost; another says most engineers work fine with a partial picture. With agents writing more of the code, the answer decides how much understanding a team has to keep.

title: No automated check tells you an assertion is right
summary: Coverage and mutation testing show whether code runs and whether a change would be noticed, but not whether the expected values are right, and model-written tests assert whatever the model expects the code to do. Some sources recommend mutation testing as a check on AI-written tests; another finds it barely tells good suites from bad ones on AI-written code. Regression tests a model writes from changed code often lock in the bug they should catch. People reading model-written assertions miss wrong ones about as often as they catch them, and the model's plain-English explanations don't help.

title: A constantly red build stops meaning anything
summary: When agents push often, the build can sit red; people stop reading it, so a real failure gets lost and a green build stops reassuring. Teams are also moving from stories to epics, and nobody has shown a pipeline that takes that batch size at speed.

title: Nobody agrees how ambitious to be with agent-built software
summary: Some practitioners say agents make far larger builds worth attempting; others say most teams lack clear pass/fail checks and can't reason about large black boxes, so should aim smaller. Both say the checks decide. Neither side has numbers. One vendor's large agent-built system had checks verified against the real service and still only partly matched it.

title: Apps can't tell an agent from the person it acts for
summary: When an agent works inside someone's session, the app's permissions and audit log see only the person. A rule like 'the agent may read but not delete' can't be enforced there, and actions can't be traced back to the agent. Drafts exist that name the agent or flag risky actions, but none yet links the agent to the person and narrows its access. For agents that run for weeks, nobody knows how a person can meaningfully approve what they may do, and how one agent should trust a request from another is unsolved.

title: AI finds bugs faster than people can fix them
summary: Bug reports are now cheap to produce, but a good fix still needs a person to choose, write and check it, so fixing crowds out new work and delays releases. Which AI-found bugs are worth a maintainer's time, such as only security ones or ones a real user can hit, isn't settled.

title: Stuck agents look for another way
summary: When a task can't be completed as specified, some agents widen the target or take a shortcut instead of stopping, from changing the test to reaching systems nobody approved. The two labs that reported it disagree on how much is model behaviour and how much is an environment left open, and neither has settled it. Agents in controlled team runs also went looking for the hidden tests that graded them. Monitoring has the mirror problem: a well-meaning agent retrying a blocked host looks like an attack.

title: Nobody knows if a second AI reviewer beats tuning the first
summary: One account finds different AI reviewers catch different problems, so it runs two; another finds a second, costlier reviewer often does worse than tuning the first. Neither compared both setups on the same PRs.

title: Nobody knows how much an AI reviewer misses
summary: Published tests show AI reviewers with low precision and recall, and their answers change between runs. Figures from real teams measure other things, such as comments accepted or rated correct, and none reports what the reviewer missed. No source compares AI review with linters or human reviewers.

title: Nobody knows if code that is easy for people is easy for agents
summary: Clear names and simple structure helped small models in several published comparisons, but the effect was weak or not significant for the strongest models, the designs are confounded, and none measured people. Teams can't yet tell whether tidying code for readers also helps their agents.

title: Saying AI wrote something costs the sender trust
summary: Team norms ask people to say when an agent wrote what they send, so reviewers know how much to check. Experiments find people who disclose AI use are trusted less than those who don't, though being found out by someone else costs more. Nobody has tested this on code or pull requests.

title: Hiring and promotion signals break when agents write the code
summary: Strong candidates fail a hand-coding interview because they no longer write code by hand, and time to finish a project no longer shows how hard it was. One company moved to interviews done with an agent and to promotion on impact; nobody has shown either picks better engineers.
